chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — _Windsor. Before PAGE’S house._
paragraphs: [Enter JUSTICE SHALLOW, SLENDER, and SIR HUGH EVANS.]
SHALLOW. Sir Hugh, don't try to talk me out of it; I'll take this all the way to the Star Chamber. If he were twenty Sir John Falstaffs, he shall not abuse Robert Shallow, Esquire.
SLENDER. Justice of the Peace in the County of Gloucester, and Coram.
SHALLOW. Yes, cousin Slender, and Custalorum.
SLENDER. Yes, and Rato-lorum too; and a gentleman born, master parson, who signs himself Armigero on any bill, warrant, receipt, or contract — Armigero.
SHALLOW. Yes, that I do; and have done for these three hundred years.
SLENDER. All his ancestors before him have done it, and all his descendants after him may do it too: they may bear the dozen white pike-fish on their coat of arms.
SHALLOW. It is an old coat.
EVANS. The dozen white louses go well with an old coat; it agrees well, passant; it is a beast familiar to man, and signifies love.
SHALLOW. The luce is the freshwater fish; the salt fish is on an old coat of arms.
SLENDER. I may quarter the arms, cousin.
SHALLOW. You may, by marrying.
EVANS. It is indeed marring, if he quarters it.
SHALLOW. Not a bit.

EVANS. Yes, by our Lady; if he takes a quarter of your coat, there is only three skirts left for yourself, by my simple reckoning. But that is all one. If Sir John Falstaff has done you wrongs, I belong to the church, and shall be glad to do my benevolence to make atonement and compromises between you.
SHALLOW. The council shall hear of it; it is a riot.

EVANS. It is not fitting for the council to hear about a riot; there is no fear of God in a riot. The council, you see, shall desire to hear of the fear of God, and not to hear of a riot. Take that into your considerations.
SHALLOW. Ha! Upon my life, if I were young again, the sword would settle it.

EVANS. It is better that friends are the sword, and settle it that way. And there is also another idea in my brain, which perhaps brings good discretions with it: there is Anne Page, who is daughter to Master Thomas Page, and she is pretty virginity.
SLENDER. Mistress Anne Page? She has brown hair, and speaks softly like a woman.

EVANS. It is exactly that person, in all the world, just as you could wish; and seven hundred pounds of money, and gold and silver, is what her grandfather on his deathbed (God grant him a joyful resurrection!) gave her, to be received when she is able to reach seventeen years old. It would be a good idea if we set aside our quibbles and quarrels, and arrange a marriage between Master Abraham and Mistress Anne Page.
SLENDER. Did her grandfather leave her seven hundred pounds?
EVANS. Yes, and her father will make her a better penny.
SLENDER. I know the young gentlewoman; she has good qualities.
EVANS. Seven hundred pounds and possibilities are good qualities.
SHALLOW. Well, let us go see honest Master Page. Is Falstaff there?

EVANS. Shall I tell you a lie? I despise a liar as I despise one who is false, or as I despise one who is not true. The knight, Sir John, is there; and I beg you, be guided by your well-wishers. I will knock on the door for Master Page.
[Knocks] What ho! God bless your house here!
PAGE. [Within] Who's there?
[Enter PAGE.]
EVANS. Here is God's blessing, and your friend, and Justice Shallow; and here is young Master Slender, who perhaps shall tell you another tale, if matters develop to your liking.
PAGE. I am glad to see your worships well. I thank you for my venison, Master Shallow.

SHALLOW. Master Page, I am glad to see you: much good may it do your good heart! I wished your venison had been better; it was poorly killed. How is good Mistress Page? — and I thank you always with my heart, indeed, with my heart.
PAGE. Sir, I thank you.
SHALLOW. Sir, I thank you; yes indeed, I do.
PAGE. I am glad to see you, good Master Slender.
SLENDER. How is your fallow greyhound, sir? I heard he was outrun on the Cotswolds.
PAGE. It could not be properly judged, sir.
SLENDER. You won't confess it, you won't confess it.
SHALLOW. He won't. It's your fault, it's your fault; it's a good dog.
PAGE. A mongrel, sir.
SHALLOW. Sir, he's a good dog, and a fine dog: can more be said? He is good and fine. Is Sir John Falstaff here?
PAGE. Sir, he is inside; and I wish I could do a good service between you.
EVANS. It is spoken as a Christian ought to speak.
SHALLOW. He has wronged me, Master Page.
PAGE. Sir, in some way he confesses it.
SHALLOW. If it is confessed, that doesn't make it right. Isn't that so, Master Page? He has wronged me; indeed he has; in a word, he has, believe me: Robert Shallow, Esquire, says he is wronged.
PAGE. Here comes Sir John.
[Enter SIR JOHN FALSTAFF, BARDOLPH, NYM, and PISTOL.]
FALSTAFF. Now, Master Shallow, you'll complain to the king about me?
SHALLOW. Sir Knight, you have beaten my men, killed my deer, and broken into my lodge.
FALSTAFF. But not kissed your gamekeeper's daughter?
SHALLOW. Pah, a trifle! This shall be answered for.
FALSTAFF. I'll answer it right now: I have done all this. There — it's answered.
SHALLOW. The council shall know about this.
FALSTAFF. It would be better for you if it were kept in confidence: you'll be laughed at.
EVANS. Pauca verba, Sir John; good words.
FALSTAFF. Good worts! Good cabbage. Slender, I broke your head: what charge do you have against me?
SLENDER. By the Virgin, sir, I have a charge in my head against you; and against your cony-catching rascals, Bardolph, Nym, and Pistol.
BARDOLPH. You Banbury cheese!
SLENDER. Yes, it doesn't matter.
PISTOL. How now, Mephostophilus!
SLENDER. Yes, it doesn't matter.
NYM. Slice, I say! Pauca, pauca: slice! That's my humour.
SLENDER. Where's Simple, my servant? Can you tell me, cousin?

EVANS. Peace, I pray you. Now let us understand. There are three umpires in this matter, as I understand it: that is, Master Page, videlicet Master Page; and there is myself, videlicet myself; and the third party is, lastly and finally, mine host of the Garter.
PAGE. We three, to hear it and end it between them.
EVANS. Very good: I will make a brief of it in my notebook; and we will afterwards work upon the case with as great discretion as we can.
FALSTAFF. Pistol!
PISTOL. He hears with ears.
EVANS. The devil and his dam! What sort of phrase is this, 'He hears with ear'? Why, it is affectation.
FALSTAFF. Pistol, did you pick Master Slender's purse?

SLENDER. Yes, by these gloves he did, or I wish I might never come into my own great chamber again — of seven groats in milled sixpences, and two Edward shovel-board coins, which cost me two shillings and twopence apiece from Yead Miller, by these gloves.
FALSTAFF. Is this true, Pistol?
EVANS. No; it is false, if it is a case of pickpocketing.
PISTOL. Ha, you mountain foreigner! Sir John and my master, I challenge this latten-bilbo to combat. Take back the lie that's on your lips here! Take it back, you froth and scum, you lie!
SLENDER. By these gloves, then, it was he.
NYM. Be advised, sir, and keep good humours: I will say 'marry trap' to you, if you run the constable's humour on me; that is the very note of it.
SLENDER. By this hat, then, the one with the red face had it; for though I can't remember what I did when you made me drunk, yet I am not altogether an ass.
FALSTAFF. What do you say, Scarlet and John?
BARDOLPH. Why, sir, for my part, I say the gentleman had drunk himself out of his five sentences.
EVANS. It is his five senses: fie, what ignorance!
BARDOLPH. And being fap, sir, was, as they say, cashiered; and so conclusions passed the careires.

SLENDER. Yes, you spoke in Latin then too; but it doesn't matter: I'll never be drunk while I live again, except in honest, civil, godly company, after this trick. If I am drunk, I'll be drunk with those who have the fear of God, and not with drunken knaves.
EVANS. So God judge me, that is a virtuous mind.
FALSTAFF. You hear all these matters denied, gentlemen; you hear it.
[Enter ANNE PAGE, with wine; MISTRESS FORD and MISTRESS PAGE, following.]
PAGE. No, daughter, carry the wine in; we'll drink inside. [Exit Anne Page.]
SLENDER. O heaven! This is Mistress Anne Page.
PAGE. How now, Mistress Ford!
FALSTAFF. Mistress Ford, by my faith, it's a fine thing to see you: with your permission, good mistress. [Kisses her.]
PAGE. Wife, make these gentlemen welcome. Come, we have a hot venison pasty for dinner: come, gentlemen, I hope we shall drink down all unkindness.
[Exeunt all except SHALLOW, SLENDER, and EVANS.]
SLENDER. I'd give forty shillings to have my Book of Songs and Sonnets here.
[Enter SIMPLE.]
How now, Simple! Where have you been? Must I wait on myself? You don't have the Book of Riddles on you, do you?
SIMPLE. Book of Riddles! Why, didn't you lend it to Alice Shortcake on All-Hallowmas last, a fortnight before Michaelmas?

SHALLOW. Come, cousin; come, cousin; we're waiting for you. A word with you, cousin: indeed, this, cousin: there is, as it were, a tender, a kind of offer, made indirectly by Sir Hugh here. Do you understand me?
SLENDER. Yes, sir, you'll find me reasonable; if it is so, I shall do what is reasonable.
SHALLOW. No, but understand me.
SLENDER. I do, sir.
EVANS. Pay attention to his propositions, Master Slender: I will describe the matter to you, if you have the capacity for it.
SLENDER. No, I will do as my cousin Shallow says: I beg you, pardon me; he's a justice of the peace in his county, simple though I stand here.
EVANS. But that is not the question: the question concerns your marriage.
SHALLOW. Yes, there's the point, sir.
EVANS. By the Virgin, that is it; the very point of it; to Mistress Anne Page.
SLENDER. Why, if that's so, I will marry her on any reasonable terms.

EVANS. But can you have affection for the woman? Let us be allowed to know that from your mouth or from your lips; for various philosophers hold that the lips are part of the mouth. Therefore, precisely, can you direct your good will toward the maid?
SHALLOW. Cousin Abraham Slender, can you love her?
SLENDER. I hope, sir, I will do as becomes one who would act reasonably.
EVANS. No, by God's lords and his ladies! You must speak positively, if you can carry your desires toward her.
SHALLOW. That you must. Will you, upon a good dowry, marry her?
SLENDER. I will do a greater thing than that, upon your request, cousin, in any reason.
SHALLOW. No, understand me, understand me, sweet cousin: what I am doing is for your pleasure, cousin. Can you love the maid?

SLENDER. I will marry her, sir, at your request: but if there is no great love in the beginning, heaven may decrease it upon better acquaintance, when we are married and have more occasion to know one another; I hope, upon familiarity will grow more contempt: but if you say 'Marry her,' I will marry her; on that point I am freely settled, and dissolutely.
EVANS. It is a very discreet answer; except that the fault is in the word 'dissolutely': the word, according to our meaning, is 'resolutely': his meaning is good.
SHALLOW. Yes, I think my cousin meant well.
SLENDER. Yes, or else I wish I might be hanged, indeed!
SHALLOW. Here comes fair Mistress Anne.
[Re-enter ANNE PAGE.]
I wish I were young for your sake, Mistress Anne!
ANNE. Dinner is on the table; my father requests your worships' company.
SHALLOW. I will attend him, fair Mistress Anne.
EVANS. By God's blessed will! I will not be absent at the grace. [Exeunt Shallow and Evans.]
ANNE. Will it please your worship to come in, sir?
SLENDER. No, I thank you, truly, with all my heart; I am very well.
ANNE. The dinner is waiting for you, sir.

SLENDER. I'm not hungry, I thank you, truly. Go, sirrah — even though you are my man, go wait on my cousin Shallow. [Exit Simple.] A justice of the peace may sometimes be obliged to his friend for a servant. I keep only three men and a boy at the moment, until my mother is dead: but what of that? I still live like a gentleman born to poverty.
ANNE. I may not go in without your worship: they won't sit down until you come.
SLENDER. In faith, I'll eat nothing; I thank you as much as if I did.
ANNE. I pray you, sir, walk in.

SLENDER. I'd rather walk out here, I thank you. I bruised my shin the other day playing at sword and dagger with a fencing master; three bouts for a dish of stewed prunes; and, by my faith, I cannot stand the smell of hot meat since. Why are your dogs barking so? Are there bears in the town?
ANNE. I think there are, sir; I've heard them talked of.
SLENDER. I love the sport well; but I shall quarrel about it as readily as any man in England. You are afraid, if you see the bear loose, are you not?
ANNE. Yes, indeed, sir.

SLENDER. That's meat and drink to me, now. I have seen Sackerson loose twenty times, and have taken him by the chain; but, I warrant you, the women have cried and shrieked so at it, that it was beyond words: but women, indeed, cannot stand them; they are very ill-favoured, rough things.
[Re-enter PAGE.]
PAGE. Come, gentle Master Slender, come; we are waiting for you.
SLENDER. I'll eat nothing, I thank you, sir.
PAGE. By cock and pie, you shall not refuse, sir! Come, come.
SLENDER. No, please, lead the way.
PAGE. Come on, sir.
SLENDER. Mistress Anne, you shall go first.
ANNE. Not I, sir; please, go on.
SLENDER. Truly, I will not go first; truly, indeed! I will not do you that wrong.
ANNE. I pray you, sir.
SLENDER. I'd rather be unmannerly than troublesome. You do yourself wrong, indeed! [Exeunt.]
NOTES: I, 1

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — _The same._
paragraphs: [Enter SIR HUGH EVANS and SIMPLE.]

EVANS. Go on your way, and ask which is the way to Doctor Caius's house: and there lives a certain Mistress Quickly, who acts as his nurse, or his dry nurse, or his cook, or his laundress — his washer, and his wringer.
SIMPLE. Yes, sir.

EVANS. No, it gets better still. Give her this letter; for she is a woman who is altogether acquainted with Mistress Anne Page: and the letter is to ask and request her to plead your master's wishes to Mistress Anne Page. I pray you, be off: I will finish my dinner; there are pippins and cheese still to come. [Exeunt.]
NOTES: I, 2

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 3 — _A room in the Garter Inn._
paragraphs: [Enter FALSTAFF, HOST, BARDOLPH, NYM, PISTOL, and ROBIN.]
FALSTAFF. My host of the Garter!
HOST. What says my swashbuckler? Speak like a scholar and wise man.
FALSTAFF. Truly, my host, I must dismiss some of my followers.
HOST. Get rid of them, bully Hercules; cashier them: let them wag off; trot, trot.
FALSTAFF. My lodging costs ten pounds a week.
HOST. You are an emperor — Caesar, Kaiser, and Pheezar. I will take on Bardolph; he shall draw drinks, he shall tap kegs: have I spoken well, bully Hector?
FALSTAFF. Do so, my good host.
HOST. I have spoken; let him follow. [To Bardolph.] Let me see you froth and water down ale: I have given my word; follow. [Exit.]
FALSTAFF. Bardolph, follow him. A tapster is a good trade: an old cloak makes a new jerkin; a worn-out servant makes a fresh tapster. Go; farewell.
BARDOLPH. It is a life I have desired: I will prosper.
PISTOL. O low Hungarian creature! Will you wield the tap?
[Exit Bardolph.]
NYM. He was conceived in drink: isn't that a clever humour?
FALSTAFF. I am glad I am rid of this tinder-box: his thefts were too open; his pilfering was like an unskillful singer — he kept no time.
NYM. The good way is to steal at a moment's rest.
PISTOL. 'Convey' — that's what the wise call it. 'Steal!' bah! a fig for that phrase!
FALSTAFF. Well, sirs, I am almost worn out at the heels.
PISTOL. Why then, let chilblains follow.
FALSTAFF. There's no remedy for it; I must catch dupes; I must scheme.
PISTOL. Young ravens must have food.
FALSTAFF. Which of you knows Ford of this town?
PISTOL. I know the man: he is of good substance.
FALSTAFF. My honest lads, I will tell you what I am up to.
PISTOL. Two yards around, and more.

FALSTAFF. No jests now, Pistol! Indeed, around the waist I am two yards; but I am now concerning no waste; I am concerned with thrift. Briefly, I mean to make love to Ford's wife: I sense entertainment in her; she discourses, she carves, she gives the look of invitation: I can interpret the meaning of her familiar style; and the toughest expression of her behaviour, to be translated rightly, is, 'I am Sir John Falstaff's.'
PISTOL. He has studied her will, and translated her will, out of honesty into English.
NYM. The anchor is deep: will that humour pass?
FALSTAFF. Now, the report goes that she has full control of her husband's purse: he has a legion of angels (gold coins).
PISTOL. As many devils to entertain her; and 'On to her, boy,' say I.
NYM. The humour rises; it is good: humour me with the angels.

FALSTAFF. I have written here a letter to her: and here another to Page's wife, who only just now gave me good looks too, examined my parts with most judicious glances; sometimes the beam of her gaze gilded my foot, sometimes my portly belly.
PISTOL. Then the sun shone on a dunghill.
NYM. I thank you for that humour.

FALSTAFF. O, she ran her eyes over my exterior with such greedy intention, that the appetite of her eye seemed to scorch me up like a burning-glass! Here's another letter to her: she controls the purse too; she is a region of Guiana, all gold and bounty. I will be a cheater to them both, and they shall be exchequers to me; they shall be my East and West Indies, and I will trade with them both. Go, you carry this letter to Mistress Page; and you this to Mistress Ford: we will prosper, lads, we will prosper.
PISTOL. Shall I become Sir Pandarus of Troy, and wear a sword at my side? Then, may Lucifer take all!
NYM. I will not run any base humour: here, take the humour-letter: I will keep the behaviour of reputation.

FALSTAFF. [To Robin] Hold, boy, bear these letters smartly; sail like my pinnace to these golden shores. Rogues, away, be gone! Vanish like hailstones, go; trudge, plod away on foot; seek shelter, pack off! Falstaff will learn the humour of the age, French thrift, you rogues; myself and my page in livery.
[Exeunt Falstaff and Robin.]
PISTOL. Let vultures grip your guts! For loaded dice rule, and high-and-low cheats both rich and poor: I'll have sixpence in my pouch when you lack, base Phrygian Turk!
NYM. I have plans which are humours of revenge.
PISTOL. Will you revenge?
NYM. By the sky and her star!
PISTOL. With wit or steel?
NYM. With both humours, I: I will reveal the humour of this love to Page.
PISTOL. And I to Ford shall also unfold how Falstaff, vile knave, will prove his dove, will hold his gold, and defile his soft couch.
NYM. My humour shall not cool: I will provoke Page to deal with poison; I will fill him with jealousy, for the outbreak of mine is dangerous: that is my true humour.
PISTOL. You are the Mars of malcontents: I second you; march on. [Exeunt.]
NOTES: I, 3

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 4 — _A room in DOCTOR CAIUS’S house._
paragraphs: [Enter MISTRESS QUICKLY, SIMPLE, and RUGBY.]

QUICKLY. What ho, John Rugby! Please go to the window and see if you can spot my master, Master Doctor Caius, coming. If he does, and he finds anybody in the house, there will be a fierce abuse of God's patience and the King's English here.
RUGBY. I'll go watch.

QUICKLY. Go; and we'll have a hot spiced drink for it later tonight, I promise, by the last embers of a sea-coal fire. [Exit Rugby.] An honest, willing, kind fellow, as ever a servant set foot in a house; and, I warrant you, no tattletale, no troublemaker. His worst fault is that he is given to prayer; he's a bit obsessive that way — but nobody is without his fault; let that pass. Peter Simple, that's your name, you say?
SIMPLE. Yes, for want of a better.
QUICKLY. And Master Slender is your master?
SIMPLE. Yes, indeed.
QUICKLY. Doesn't he wear a great round beard, like a glover's paring-knife?
SIMPLE. No, indeed: he has only a little tiny face, with a little yellow beard — a Cain-coloured beard.
QUICKLY. A meek-spirited man, isn't he?
SIMPLE. Yes, indeed: but he is as tough a man with his fists as anybody you'll find between here and his own head; he has fought with a warrener.
QUICKLY. How's that? — Oh, I should remember him: doesn't he hold his head up high, and swagger as he walks?
SIMPLE. Yes, indeed, he does.
QUICKLY. Well, may heaven send Anne Page no worse fortune! Tell Master Parson Evans I will do what I can for your master: Anne is a good girl, and I wish—
[Re-enter RUGBY.]
RUGBY. Quick, alas! Here comes my master.
QUICKLY. We shall all catch it. Run in here, good young man; go into this closet: he will not stay long.
[Shuts SIMPLE in the closet.] What ho, John Rugby! John!
What, John, I say! Go, John, go ask after my master; I'm afraid he isn't well, since he hasn't come home.
[Singing] And down, down, adown-a, etc.
[Enter DOCTOR CAIUS.]
CAIUS. What is you sing? I do not like dese toys. Please, go and fetch me in my closet un boitier vert — a box, a green-a box: do you understand what I speak? A green-a box.
QUICKLY. Yes, indeed; I'll fetch it for you. [Aside] I am glad he did not go in himself: if he had found the young man, he would have gone raving mad.
CAIUS. Fie, fie, fie, fie! Upon my faith, it is very hot. I am going to the court — on a great matter.
QUICKLY. Is it this, sir?
CAIUS. Yes; put it in my pocket: hurry, quickly. Where is dat knave Rugby?
QUICKLY. What ho, John Rugby! John!
RUGBY. Here, sir!
CAIUS. You are John Rugby, and you are Jack Rugby. Come, take your rapier, and come at my heels to the court.
RUGBY. It's ready, sir, here in the porch.
CAIUS. By my troth, I tarry too long. — Goodness me! What did I forget! There are some herbs in my closet that I would not for the world leave behind.
QUICKLY. Oh dear, he'll find the young man there, and go mad!
CAIUS. Oh devil, devil! What is in my closet? Villain! Thief! [Pulling SIMPLE out.] Rugby, my rapier!
QUICKLY. Good master, calm yourself.
CAIUS. Why should I be calm?
QUICKLY. The young man is an honest man.
CAIUS. What shall an honest man do in my closet? There is no honest man dat shall come in my closet.
QUICKLY. I beg you, don't be so worked up. Hear the truth of it: he came on an errand to me from Parson Hugh.
CAIUS. Well.
SIMPLE. Yes, indeed; to ask her to—
QUICKLY. Hush, please.
CAIUS. Hush your own tongue. Speak your tale.
SIMPLE. To ask this honest gentlewoman, your maid, to speak a good word to Mistress Anne Page for my master with a view to marriage.
QUICKLY. That is all, indeed, truly! But I'll never put my finger in the fire when I don't have to.
CAIUS. Sir Hugh sent you? Rugby, bring me some paper. Wait a little while. [Writes.]

QUICKLY. [Aside to SIMPLE] I am glad he is so quiet: if he had been thoroughly worked up, you would have heard him going on so loud and so melancholy. But notwithstanding, my man, I'll do your master what good I can: and the very yes and the no of it is, the French doctor, my master — I may call him my master, look you, for I keep his house; and I wash, wring, brew, bake, scour, dress meat and drink, make the beds, and do everything myself—
SIMPLE. [Aside to QUICKLY] It's a great burden to come under one person's hand.

QUICKLY. [Aside to SIMPLE] Are you aware of that? You'll find it a great burden: and to be up early and down late — but notwithstanding — to tell you in your ear; I would have no word of this — my master himself is in love with Mistress Anne Page: but in spite of that, I know Anne's mind — that's neither here nor there.

CAIUS. You jackanapes, give this letter to Sir Hugh; by God, it is a challenge: I will cut his throat in the park; and I will teach a scurvy jackanapes priest to meddle and intrude. You may be gone; it is not good that you tarry here. — By God, I will cut off both his stones; by God, he shall not have a stone to throw at his dog. [Exit SIMPLE.]
QUICKLY. Alas, he speaks only for his friend.

CAIUS. It is no matter for that: — did you not tell me that I shall have Anne Page for myself? — By God, I will kill the Jack priest; and I have appointed mine host of the Garter to measure our weapons: — By God, I will have Anne Page myself.
QUICKLY. Sir, the maid loves you, and all shall be well. We must let folks chatter on: what, the mischief!
CAIUS. Rugby, come to the court with me. By God, if I do not have Anne Page, I shall turn your head out of my door. Follow my heels, Rugby. [Exeunt CAIUS and RUGBY.]
QUICKLY. You shall have a fool's head of your own. No, I know Anne's mind as well as that: no woman in Windsor knows more of Anne's mind than I do; nor can do more than I do with her, I thank heaven.
FENTON. [Within] Who's there inside? Hello!
QUICKLY. Who's there, I wonder? Come closer to the house, please.
[Enter FENTON.]
FENTON. How now, good woman! How do you do?
QUICKLY. The better for your good worship asking.
FENTON. What news? How does pretty Mistress Anne?
QUICKLY. In truth, sir, she is pretty, and honest, and gentle; and one that is your friend, I can tell you that by the way; I praise heaven for it.
FENTON. Shall I have any success, do you think? Shall I not lose my suit?
QUICKLY. Truly, sir, all is in his hands above: but notwithstanding, Master Fenton, I'll swear on a book that she loves you. Doesn't your worship have a wart above your eye?
FENTON. Yes, indeed, I do; what of that?

QUICKLY. Well, thereby hangs a tale: — in good faith, she is such another Nan; but, I protest, an honest maid as ever broke bread: — we had an hour's talk about that wart. — I shall never laugh except in that maid's company! — But, indeed, she is too much given to melancholy and brooding: but as for you — well, go to.
FENTON. Well, I shall see her today. Here, take this money; let me have your good word on my behalf: if you see her before me, commend me to her.
QUICKLY. Will I? Indeed, that I will; and I will tell your worship more of the wart the next time we have a private talk; and of other suitors.
FENTON. Well, farewell; I am in great haste now.
QUICKLY. Farewell to your worship. [Exit FENTON.] Truly, an honest gentleman: but Anne doesn't love him; for I know Anne's mind as well as anybody. — Confound it! What have I forgotten? [Exit.]
NOTES: I, 4

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — _Before PAGE’S house._
paragraphs: [Enter MISTRESS PAGE, with a letter.]
[Transcriber's Note: In order to preserve the marked line breaks without losing readability, each line of the quoted letter has been split into two equal halves.]
MISTRESS PAGE. What, have I escaped love-letters in the holiday-time of my beauty, only to become a target for them now? Let me see. [Reads:]

'Ask me no reason why I love you; for though Love uses Reason for his physician, he does not admit him as his counsellor. You are not young, no more am I; well then, there's a sympathy: you are merry, so am I; ha, ha! Then there's more sympathy: you love sack, and so do I; could you wish for better sympathy? Let it suffice you, Mistress Page — at the very least, if a soldier's love can suffice — that I love you. I will not say, pity me — that is no soldier's phrase; but I say, love me. By me,
Your own true knight, by day or by night, or any kind of light, with all his might for you to fight, JOHN FALSTAFF.'

What a Herod of Jewry is this! O wicked, wicked world! A man almost worn to pieces with age — playing the young gallant! What thoughtless behaviour of mine has this Flemish drunkard picked up — in the devil's name! — out of my conversation, that he dares assault me in this fashion? Why, he has not been in my company three times! What shall I say to him? I was sparing of my mirth then: heaven forgive me! Why, I'll submit a bill to parliament for the putting down of men. How shall I be revenged on him? for revenged I will be, as surely as his guts are made of puddings.
[Enter MISTRESS FORD.]
MISTRESS FORD. Mistress Page! Trust me, I was on my way to your house.
MISTRESS PAGE. And trust me, I was coming to you. You look very ill.
MISTRESS FORD. No, I'll never believe that; I can show the contrary.
MISTRESS PAGE. Faith, but you do, in my opinion.
MISTRESS FORD. Well, I do, then; yet I say, I could show you the contrary. O Mistress Page, give me some counsel!
MISTRESS PAGE. What's the matter, woman?
MISTRESS FORD. O woman, if it weren't for one trifling matter, I could come to such honour!
MISTRESS PAGE. Hang the trifle, woman! Take the honour. What is it? — never mind the trifles — what is it?
MISTRESS FORD. If I would just go to hell for an eternal moment or so, I could be knighted.
MISTRESS PAGE. What? You lie! Sir Alice Ford! These knights will turn out badly; so you shouldn't alter the article of your gentry.

MISTRESS FORD. We're wasting daylight: — here, read, read; see how I might be knighted. I shall think the worse of fat men, as long as I have an eye to distinguish men's looks: and yet he would not swear; he praised women's modesty; and gave such orderly and well-mannered reproof to all unseemliness, that I would have sworn his disposition matched the truth of his words; but they hold together no more than the Hundredth Psalm to the tune of 'Green Sleeves.' What tempest, I wonder, threw this whale, with so many tons of oil in his belly, ashore at Windsor? How shall I be revenged on him? I think the best way were to entertain him with hope, until the wicked fire of lust has melted him in his own grease. Did you ever hear the like?

MISTRESS PAGE. Letter for letter — except that the names of Page and Ford are different! To your great comfort in this riddle of ill thoughts, here is the twin-brother of your letter: but let yours inherit first; for, I protest, mine never shall. I warrant he has a thousand of these letters, written with blank space for different names — surely more — and these are of the second edition: he will print them, no doubt; for he cares nothing what he puts into the press, when he would put both of us into it. I would rather be a giantess, and lie under Mount Pelion. Well, I will find you twenty lustful turtle-doves before one chaste man.
MISTRESS FORD. Why, this is the very same; the very hand, the very words. What does he think of us?

MISTRESS PAGE. No, I don't know: it makes me almost ready to quarrel with my own honesty. I'll treat myself like someone I'm not acquainted with; for, surely, unless he knows some strain in me that I don't know myself, he would never have boarded me in such a fury.
MISTRESS FORD. 'Boarding,' do you call it? I'll be sure to keep him above deck.

MISTRESS PAGE. So will I: if he comes under my hatches, I'll never go to sea again. Let's be revenged on him: let's arrange a meeting with him; give him a show of encouragement in his suit, and lead him on with a fine baited delay, until he has pawned his horses to the host of the Garter.
MISTRESS FORD. No, I will agree to act any villainy against him, that may not stain the carefulness of our honesty. O, if only my husband saw this letter! It would give eternal food to his jealousy.
MISTRESS PAGE. Why, look where he comes; and my good man too: he is as far from jealousy as I am from giving him cause; and that, I hope, is an immeasurable distance.
MISTRESS FORD. You are the happier woman.
MISTRESS PAGE. Let's plot together against this greasy knight. Come over here. [They retire.]
[Enter FORD with PISTOL, and PAGE with NYM.]
FORD. Well, I hope it is not so.
PISTOL. Hope is a curtailed dog in some matters: Sir John has designs on your wife.
FORD. Why, sir, my wife is not young.
PISTOL. He woos both high and low, both rich and poor, both young and old, all together, Ford; he loves the gallimaufry: Ford, consider.
FORD. Love my wife!
PISTOL. With liver burning hot. Prevent it, or you'll go like Sir Actaeon, with Ringwood at your heels: O, hateful is the name!
FORD. What name, sir?

PISTOL. The horn, I say. Farewell. Take heed; keep an open eye; for thieves walk by night: take heed, before summer comes, or cuckoo birds sing. Away, Sir Corporal Nym! — Believe him, Page; he speaks sense. [Exit.]
FORD. [Aside] I will be patient; I will find this out.

NYM. [To PAGE] And this is true; I do not like the humour of lying. He has wronged me in some humours: I should have carried the humoured letter to her; but I have a sword, and it shall bite when I need it. He loves your wife; that's the short and the long of it. My name is Corporal Nym; I speak and I vouch; 'tis true: my name is Nym, and Falstaff loves your wife. Farewell. I do not love the humour of bread and cheese [and there's the humour of it]. Farewell. [Exit.]
PAGE. 'The humour of it,' says he! Here's a fellow who frightens English out of its wits.
FORD. I will seek out Falstaff.
PAGE. I never heard such a drawling, affected rogue.
FORD. If I find it to be true: — well.
PAGE. I would not believe such a Cataian, even if the priest of the town vouched for him as a true man.
FORD. He was a sensible fellow: — well.
PAGE. How now, Meg!
[MISTRESS PAGE and MISTRESS FORD come forward.]
MISTRESS PAGE. Where are you going, George? Listen to me.
MISTRESS FORD. How now, sweet Frank! Why are you melancholy?
FORD. I melancholy! I am not melancholy. Go home, go.
MISTRESS FORD. Faith, you have some odd notions in your head. Now, will you come, Mistress Page?
MISTRESS PAGE. I'll come along. You'll come to dinner, George? [Aside to MISTRESS FORD] Look who comes yonder: she shall be our messenger to this paltry knight.
MISTRESS FORD. [Aside to MISTRESS PAGE] Trust me, I thought of her: she'll fit the role.
[Enter MISTRESS QUICKLY.]
MISTRESS PAGE. You've come to see my daughter Anne?
QUICKLY. Yes, indeed; and, please, how does good Mistress Anne?
MISTRESS PAGE. Come in with us and see: we shall have an hour's talk with you.
[Exeunt MISTRESS PAGE, MISTRESS FORD, and MISTRESS QUICKLY.]
PAGE. How now, Master Ford!
FORD. You heard what this knave told me, did you not?
PAGE. Yes: and you heard what the other told me?
FORD. Do you think there is truth in what they said?

PAGE. Hang them, knaves! I don't think the knight would attempt it: but those who accuse him of designs on our wives are a pair of his dismissed men; downright rogues, now that they are out of service.
FORD. Were they his men?
PAGE. Indeed they were.
FORD. That makes me like it no better. Does he stay at the Garter?
PAGE. Yes, indeed, he does. If he should mean to launch this voyage toward my wife, I would turn her loose on him; and whatever he gets from her beyond sharp words, let it lie on my head.
FORD. I do not suspect my wife; but I would be loath to throw them together. A man may be too confident: I would have nothing lie on my head: I cannot be so satisfied.
PAGE. Look where my blustering host of the Garter comes: there is either liquor in his head, or money in his purse, when he looks so merry.
[Enter HOST.]
How now, my host!
HOST. How now, swashbuckler! You're a gentleman. Cavaleiro-justice, I say!
[Enter SHALLOW.]
SHALLOW. I follow, my host, I follow. Good evening, and twenty more, good Master Page! Master Page, will you go with us? We have some sport in hand.
HOST. Tell him, cavaleiro-justice; tell him, swashbuckler.
SHALLOW. Sir, there is a fight to be fought between Sir Hugh the Welsh priest and Caius the French doctor.
FORD. Good host of the Garter, a word with you.
[Drawing him aside.]
HOST. What do you say, my swashbuckler?

SHALLOW. [To PAGE] Will you go with us to watch it? My merry host has had the measuring of their weapons; and, I think, has appointed them to opposite places; for, believe me, I hear the parson is no jester. Hark, I will tell you what our sport shall be. [They converse apart.]
HOST. Have you no suit against my knight, my guest-cavalier?
FORD. None, I protest: but I'll give you a quart of burnt sack to give me access to him, and tell him my name is Brook; only for a jest.
HOST. My hand, swashbuckler; you shall have free coming and going — did I speak well? — and your name shall be Brook. He is a merry knight. Will you go, my heirs?
SHALLOW. I'll come along, my host.
PAGE. I have heard the Frenchman has good skill with his rapier.

SHALLOW. Tut, sir, I could have told you more. In these times you fight by distance, with your passes, stoccadoes, and I know not what else: it's the heart, Master Page; it's here, it's here. I've seen the time when, with my long sword, I would have made four tall fellows like you skip like rats.
HOST. Here, boys, here, here! Shall we be off?
PAGE. I'll come. I would rather hear them scold than fight. [Exeunt HOST, SHALLOW, and PAGE.]

FORD. Though Page is a complacent fool, and stands so firmly on his wife's faithfulness, I cannot put off my suspicion so easily: she was in his company at Page's house; and what they did there, I do not know. Well, I will look further into it: and I have a disguise with which to sound out Falstaff. If I find her honest, I lose nothing for my labour; if she be otherwise, it's labour well spent. [Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 2 — _A room in the Garter Inn._
paragraphs: [Enter FALSTAFF and PISTOL.]
FALSTAFF. I will not lend you a penny.
PISTOL. Why, then the world's my oyster, which I with sword will open.

FALSTAFF. Not a penny. I have been content, sir, to let you pawn my good name: I have pestered my good friends for three reprieves for you and your coach-fellow Nym; or else you would have looked through prison bars, like a pair of baboons. I am damned in hell for swearing to my gentlemen friends that you were good soldiers and brave fellows; and when Mistress Bridget lost the handle of her fan, I swore on my honour you didn't have it.
PISTOL. Didn't you share? Didn't you get fifteen pence?

FALSTAFF. With reason, you rogue, with reason: do you think I'll endanger my soul for free? In a word, hang no more about me; I am no gibbet for you. Go. A short knife and a crowd! — To your manor of Pickt-hatch! Go. You will not carry a letter for me, you rogue! You stand upon your honour! Why, you boundless lowness, it is as much as I can do to keep my honour precise: I, I, I myself sometimes — leaving the fear of God on the left hand, and hiding my honour in my necessity — am forced to shuffle, hedge, and lurch; and yet you, rogue, will conceal your rags, your cat-a-mountain looks, your tavern phrases, and your bold-faced oaths under the shelter of your honour! You won't do it, you!
PISTOL. I relent: what more would you want from a man?
[Enter ROBIN.]
ROBIN. Sir, here's a woman who would speak with you.
FALSTAFF. Let her approach.
[Enter MISTRESS QUICKLY.]
QUICKLY. Good morrow to your worship.
FALSTAFF. Good morrow, good wife.
QUICKLY. Not so, if it please your worship.
FALSTAFF. Good maid, then.
QUICKLY. I'll swear to it; as my mother was, the first hour I was born.
FALSTAFF. I believe the swearer. What do you want with me?
QUICKLY. May I grant your worship a word or two?
FALSTAFF. Two thousand, fair woman: and I'll grant you the hearing.
QUICKLY. There is one Mistress Ford, sir: — please, come a little nearer this way: — I myself dwell with Master Doctor Caius—
FALSTAFF. Well, go on: Mistress Ford, you say—
QUICKLY. Your worship says very true: — please, your worship, come a little nearer this way.
FALSTAFF. I warrant you, nobody hears; — my own people, my own people.
QUICKLY. Are they so? God bless them, and make them his servants!
FALSTAFF. Well, Mistress Ford; — what of her?
QUICKLY. Why, sir, she's a good creature. — Lord, Lord! Your worship is a wanton! Well, heaven forgive you and all of us, I pray!
FALSTAFF. Mistress Ford; — come, Mistress Ford—

QUICKLY. Indeed, this is the short and the long of it: you have brought her into such a flutter as is wonderful. The best courtier of them all, when the court was at Windsor, could never have brought her to such a flutter. Yet there have been knights, and lords, and gentlemen, with their coaches; I warrant you, coach after coach, letter after letter, gift after gift; smelling so sweetly, all musk, and rustling, I warrant you, in silk and gold; and in such elegant terms; and in such wine and sugar of the best and the fairest, that would have won any woman's heart; and, I warrant you, they could never get an eye-wink from her: I had twenty angels given me this morning myself; but I defy all angels — in any such sort, as they say — except in the way of honesty: and, I warrant you, they could never get her so much as to sip on a cup with the proudest of them all: and yet there have been earls, indeed, what's more, pensioners; but, I warrant you, all is one with her.
FALSTAFF. But what does she say to me? Be brief, my good she-Mercury.
QUICKLY. Indeed, she has received your letter; for which she thanks you a thousand times; and she gives you notice that her husband will be away from his house between ten and eleven.
FALSTAFF. Ten and eleven.

QUICKLY. Yes, indeed; and then you may come and see the picture, she says, that you know about: Master Ford, her husband, will be away from home. Alas, the sweet woman leads an ill life with him! He's a very jealous man: she leads a very vexed life with him, good heart.
FALSTAFF. Ten and eleven. Woman, commend me to her; I will not fail her.

QUICKLY. Why, you say well. But I have another message for your worship. Mistress Page sends her hearty commendations to you, too: and let me tell you in your ear, she's as virtuous a civil modest wife — and one, I tell you, who will not miss morning or evening prayer — as any woman in Windsor, whoever the other may be: and she bade me tell your worship that her husband is seldom away from home; but, she hopes, the time will come. I never knew a woman so dote upon a man: surely, I think you have charms; yes, in truth.
FALSTAFF. Not I, I assure you: setting aside the attraction of my good parts, I have no other charms.
QUICKLY. Blessings on your heart for that!
FALSTAFF. But please, tell me this: has Ford's wife and Page's wife let each other know how much they love me?

QUICKLY. That would be a jest indeed! They have not so little grace as that, I hope: that would be a trick indeed! But Mistress Page asks you most lovingly to send her your little page: her husband has a marvellous fondness for the little page; and, truly, Master Page is an honest man. Never a wife in Windsor leads a better life than she does: do what she will, say what she will, take all, pay all, go to bed when she likes, rise when she likes, all is as she wishes: and, truly, she deserves it; for if there is a kind woman in Windsor, she is one. You must send her your page; no help for it.
FALSTAFF. Why, I will.

QUICKLY. No, but do so, then: and, look you, he may come and go between you both; and, in any case, have a code-word, so that you may know each other's mind, and the boy need never understand anything; for it is not good that children should know any wickedness: old folks, you know, have discretion, as they say, and know the world.
FALSTAFF. Farewell: commend me to them both: there's my purse; I am still your debtor. Boy, go along with this woman. [Exeunt MISTRESS QUICKLY and ROBIN.] This news distracts me!
PISTOL. This wench is one of Cupid's carriers: clap on more sails; pursue; up with your fights: give fire: she is my prize, or let the ocean overwhelm them all! [Exit.]

FALSTAFF. Do you say so, old Jack? Go your ways; I'll make more of your old body than I've done so far. Will they still look after you? Will you, after the expense of so much money, now be a gainer? Good body, I thank you. Let them say it is grossly done; so long as it is fairly done, no matter.
[Enter BARDOLPH.]
BARDOLPH. Sir John, there is one Master Brook below who would gladly speak with you, and be acquainted with you; and he has sent your worship a morning draught of sack.
FALSTAFF. Brook is his name?
BARDOLPH. Yes, sir.
FALSTAFF. Call him in. [Exit BARDOLPH.] Such Brooks are welcome to me, that overflow with such liquor. Aha! Mistress Ford and Mistress Page — have I cornered you? Go to; on we go!
[Re-enter BARDOLPH, with FORD disguised.]
FORD. Bless you, sir!
FALSTAFF. And you, sir! Would you speak with me?
FORD. I take the liberty of intruding on you with so little preparation.
FALSTAFF. You're welcome. What's your wish? — Leave us, drawer. [Exit BARDOLPH.]
FORD. Sir, I am a gentleman who has spent much; my name is Brook.
FALSTAFF. Good Master Brook, I desire further acquaintance with you.

FORD. Good Sir John, I sue for yours: not to be a charge on you; for I must let you understand that I think myself in better condition as a lender than you are: which has somewhat emboldened me to this untimely intrusion; for they say, if money goes before, all ways lie open.
FALSTAFF. Money is a good soldier, sir, and will go on.
FORD. Truly, and I have a bag of money here that troubles me: if you will help to bear it, Sir John, take all, or half, to ease me of the carriage.
FALSTAFF. Sir, I do not know how I may deserve to be your porter.
FORD. I will tell you, sir, if you will give me the hearing.
FALSTAFF. Speak, good Master Brook: I shall be glad to be your servant.

FORD. Sir, I hear you are a scholar — I will be brief with you — and you have been a man long known to me, though I never had so good means, as I had desire, to make myself acquainted with you. I shall reveal something to you, in which I must very much lay open my own imperfection: but, good Sir John, as you keep one eye upon my follies as you hear them unfolded, turn another to the register of your own; so that I may pass with a reproof more easily, since you yourself know how easy it is to be such an offender.
FALSTAFF. Very well, sir; proceed.
FORD. There is a gentlewoman in this town; her husband's name is Ford.
FALSTAFF. Well, sir.

FORD. I have long loved her, and, I protest to you, bestowed much on her; followed her with a doting attentiveness; engrossed every opportunity to meet her; paid for every slight occasion that could but stingily give me a glimpse of her; not only bought many presents to give her, but have paid handsomely to many to know what she would have given; briefly, I have pursued her as love has pursued me; which has been on the wing of every opportunity. But whatever I have merited, either in my mind or in my means, in reward, I am sure, I have received none; unless experience be a jewel that I have purchased at an infinite rate, and which has taught me to say this: 'Love like a shadow flies when substance love pursues; pursuing that which flies, and flying what pursues.'
FALSTAFF. Have you received no promise of satisfaction at her hands?
FORD. Never.
FALSTAFF. Have you pressed her to that purpose?
FORD. Never.
FALSTAFF. Of what quality was your love, then?
FORD. Like a fair house built on another man's ground; so that I have lost my edifice by mistaking the place where I erected it.
FALSTAFF. To what purpose have you unfolded this to me?

FORD. When I have told you that, I have told you everything. Some say, that although she appears honest to me, yet in other places she lets her mirth run so far that there is shrewd interpretation made of her. Now, Sir John, here is the heart of my purpose: you are a gentleman of excellent breeding, admirable discourse, great social access, authentic in your place and person, generally allowed for your many warlike, courtly, and learned accomplishments.
FALSTAFF. O, sir!

FORD. Believe it, for you know it. There is money; spend it, spend it; spend more; spend all I have; only give me so much of your time in exchange for it, as to lay an amorous siege to the honesty of this Ford's wife: use your art of wooing; win her to consent to you: if any man can, you can as soon as any.
FALSTAFF. Would it suit the vehemence of your affection that I should win what you would enjoy? It seems to me you prescribe for yourself very preposterously.

FORD. O, understand my drift. She dwells so securely on the excellence of her honour, that the folly of my soul dares not present itself: she is too bright to be looked upon. Now, if I could come to her with any evidence in my hand, my desires would have grounds and arguments to recommend themselves: I could drive her then from the defence of her purity, her reputation, her marriage-vow, and a thousand other defences of hers, which now are too, too strongly arrayed against me. What do you say to it, Sir John?
FALSTAFF. Master Brook, I will first make bold with your money; next, give me your hand; and last, as I am a gentleman, you shall, if you will, enjoy Ford's wife.
FORD. O good sir!
FALSTAFF. I say you shall.
FORD. Want no money, Sir John; you shall want none.

FALSTAFF. Want no Mistress Ford, Master Brook; you shall want none. I shall be with her, I may tell you, by her own appointment; even as you came in to me, her go-between parted from me: I say I shall be with her between ten and eleven; for at that time the jealous rascally knave her husband will be out. Come to me tonight; you shall know how I succeed.
FORD. I am blessed in your acquaintance. Do you know Ford, sir?

FALSTAFF. Hang him, poor cuckoldly knave! I do not know him: — yet I wrong him to call him poor; they say the jealous wittol knave has masses of money; for which his wife seems well-favoured to me. I will use her as the key of the cuckoldly rogue's coffer; and there's my harvest-home.
FORD. I would you knew Ford, sir, that you might avoid him, if you saw him.

FALSTAFF. Hang him, low-born salt-butter rogue! I will stare him out of his wits; I will overawe him with my cudgel: it shall hang like a meteor over the cuckold's horns. Master Brook, you shall know I will lord it over the peasant, and you shall lie with his wife. — Come to me soon tonight. Ford's a knave, and I will pile up his titles; you, Master Brook, shall know him for knave and cuckold. Come to me soon tonight. [Exit.]

FORD. What a damned Epicurean rascal this is! My heart is ready to crack with impatience. Who says this is foolish jealousy? My wife has sent to him; the hour is fixed; the match is made. Would any man have thought this? See the hell of having a false woman! My bed shall be abused, my coffers ransacked, my reputation gnawed at; and I shall not only receive this villainous wrong, but stand under the burden of abominable names, and by the man who does me this wrong. Names! Names! — Amaimon sounds well; Lucifer, well; Barbason, well; yet they are devils' titles, the names of fiends: but Cuckold! Wittol! — Cuckold! The devil himself has no such name. Page is an ass, a complacent ass: he will trust his wife; he will not be jealous. I would sooner trust a Fleming with my butter, Parson Hugh the Welshman with my cheese, an Irishman with my aqua-vitae bottle, or a thief to walk my ambling gelding, than my wife with herself: then she plots, then she ruminates, then she devises; and what they think in their hearts they may bring about, they will break their hearts but they will bring it about. God be praised for my jealousy! — Eleven o'clock the hour. I will prevent this, detect my wife, be revenged on Falstaff, and laugh at Page. I'll go about it; better three hours too soon than a minute too late. Fie, fie, fie! Cuckold! Cuckold! Cuckold! [Exit.]
NOTES: II, 2

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 3 — _A field near Windsor._
paragraphs: [Enter CAIUS and RUGBY.]
CAIUS. Jack Rugby!
RUGBY. Sir?
CAIUS. What is the clock, Jack?
RUGBY. It's past the hour, sir, that Sir Hugh promised to meet.
CAIUS. By God, he has saved his soul, that he is no come; he has prayed his Bible well, that he is no come: by God, Jack Rugby, he is dead already, if he be come.
RUGBY. He is wise, sir; he knew your worship would kill him, if he came.
CAIUS. By God, the herring is no dead so as I will kill him. Take your rapier, Jack; I will tell you how I will kill him.
RUGBY. Alas, sir, I cannot fence.
CAIUS. Villainy, take your rapier.
RUGBY. Hold off; here's company.
[Enter HOST, SHALLOW, SLENDER, and PAGE.]
HOST. Bless you, swashbuckler doctor!
SHALLOW. God save you, Master Doctor Caius!
PAGE. Well met, good master doctor!
SLENDER. Good morrow to you, sir.
CAIUS. What be all you, one, two, tree, four, come for?

HOST. To see you fight, to see you thrust, to see you traverse; to see you here, to see you there; to see you make your punto, your stock, your reverse, your distance, your montant. Is he dead, my Ethiopian? Is he dead, my Francisco? Ha, swashbuckler! What says my Aesculapius? My Galen? My heart of elder? Ha! Is he dead, bully-stale? Is he dead?
CAIUS. By God, he is the coward Jack priest of the world; he is not show his face.
HOST. You are a Castalion-King-Urinal. Hector of Greece, my boy!
CAIUS. I pray you, bear witness that me have stay six or seven, two, tree hours for him, and he is no come.
SHALLOW. He is the wiser man, master doctor: he is a curer of souls, and you a curer of bodies; if you should fight, you go against the hair of your professions. Is it not true, Master Page?
PAGE. Master Shallow, you have yourself been a great fighter, though now a man of peace.

SHALLOW. By God's body, Master Page, though I am now old, and of the peace, if I see a sword out, my finger itches to wield one. Though we are justices, and doctors, and churchmen, Master Page, we have some salt of our youth in us; we are the sons of women, Master Page.
PAGE. That's true, Master Shallow.

SHALLOW. It will be found so, Master Page. Master Doctor Caius, I have come to fetch you home. I am sworn to the peace: you have shown yourself a wise physician, and Sir Hugh has shown himself a wise and patient churchman. You must go with me, master doctor.
HOST. Pardon, guest-justice. — A word, Monsieur Mock-water.
CAIUS. Mock-vater! What is that?
HOST. Mock-water, in our English tongue, is valour, swashbuckler.
CAIUS. By God, then, I have as much mock-vater as the Englishman. — Scurvy jack-dog priest! By God, me will cut his ears.
HOST. He will scratch and claw you tightly, swashbuckler.
CAIUS. Clapper-de-claw! What is that?
HOST. That is, he will make amends to you.
CAIUS. By God, me do look he shall clapper-de-claw me; for, by God, me will have it.
HOST. And I will provoke him to it, or let him be off.
CAIUS. Me thank you for that.
HOST. And, moreover, swashbuckler — But first, master guest, and Master Page, and also Cavaleiro Slender, you go through the town to Frogmore. [Aside to them.]
PAGE. Sir Hugh is there, is he?
HOST. He is there: see what humour he is in; and I will bring the doctor round by the fields. Will it do well?
SHALLOW. We will do it.
PAGE, SHALLOW, and SLENDER. Farewell, good master doctor.
[Exeunt PAGE, SHALLOW, and SLENDER.]
CAIUS. By God, me will kill the priest; for he speak for a jackanapes to Anne Page.

HOST. Let him die: sheathe your impatience, throw cold water on your anger: come about the fields with me through Frogmore: I will bring you where Mistress Anne Page is, at a farmhouse feasting; and you shall woo her. Did I hit the mark? Did I speak well?
CAIUS. By God, me thank you for that: by God, I love you; and I shall procure you the good guest, the earl, the knight, the lords, the gentlemen, my patients.
HOST. For which I will be your champion in the suit for Anne Page. Did I speak well?
CAIUS. By God, it is good; well said.
HOST. Let us be off, then.
CAIUS. Come at my heels, Jack Rugby. [Exeunt.]
NOTES: II, 3

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — _A field near Frogmore._
paragraphs: [Enter SIR HUGH EVANS and SIMPLE.]
EVANS. I pray you now, good Master Slender's serving-man, and friend Simple by your name, which way have you looked for Master Caius, that calls himself doctor of physic?
SIMPLE. Indeed, sir, towards the pittie-ward, towards the park, every way; the old Windsor way, and every way but the town way.
EVANS. I most vehemently desire you will also look that way.
SIMPLE. I will, sir. [Exit.]

EVANS. Bless my soul, how full of choler I am, and trembling of mind! — I shall be glad if he has deceived me. — How melancholy I am! — I will knock his urinals about his knave's head when I have good opportunities for the work. — Bless my soul! — [Sings.]
To shallow rivers, to whose falls melodious birds sing madrigals; there will we make our beds of roses, and a thousand fragrant posies. To shallow—
Mercy on me! I have a great disposition to cry. [Sings.]
Melodious birds sing madrigals — Whenas I sat in Babylon — and a thousand vagrant posies. To shallow, etc.
[Re-enter SIMPLE.]
SIMPLE. Yonder he comes, this way, Sir Hugh.
EVANS. He's welcome. — [Sings.]
To shallow rivers, to whose falls—
Heaven prosper the right! — What weapons does he have?
SIMPLE. No weapons, sir. There comes my master, Master Shallow, and another gentleman, from Frogmore, over the stile, this way.
EVANS. Please, give me my gown; or else keep it in your arms.
[Enter PAGE, SHALLOW, and SLENDER.]
SHALLOW. How now, master parson! Good morrow, good Sir Hugh. Keep a gambler from the dice, and a good student from his book, and it is wonderful.
SLENDER. [Aside] Ah, sweet Anne Page!
PAGE. God save you, good Sir Hugh!
EVANS. Bless you, for his mercy's sake, all of you!
SHALLOW. What, the sword and the word! Do you study them both, master parson?
PAGE. And youthful still! In your doublet and hose this raw rheumatic day!
EVANS. There are reasons and causes for it.
PAGE. We have come to you to do a good office, master parson.
EVANS. Very well: what is it?
PAGE. Yonder is a most reverend gentleman, who, likely having received some wrong by some person, is at the most odds with his own gravity and patience that you ever saw.
SHALLOW. I have lived fourscore years and more; I have never heard a man of his rank, gravity, and learning, so far from his own self-respect.
EVANS. Who is he?
PAGE. I think you know him: Master Doctor Caius, the renowned French physician.
EVANS. God's will, and his passion in my heart! I had as soon you would tell me of a mess of porridge.
PAGE. Why?
EVANS. He has no more knowledge of Hippocrates and Galen — and he is a knave besides; as cowardly a knave as you would desire to be acquainted with.
PAGE. I warrant you, he is the man who is to fight with him.
SLENDER. [Aside] O sweet Anne Page!
SHALLOW. It appears so, by his weapons. Keep them apart: here comes Doctor Caius.
[Enter HOST, CAIUS, and RUGBY.]
PAGE. No, good master parson, sheathe your weapon.
SHALLOW. So do you, good master doctor.
HOST. Disarm them, and let them argue: let them keep their limbs whole, and hack our English.
CAIUS. I pray you, let me speak a word with your ear. Vere-fore vill you not meet me?
EVANS. [Aside to CAIUS] Please, use your patience: in good time.
CAIUS. By God, you are the coward, the Jack-dog, John-ape.
EVANS. [Aside to CAIUS] Please, let us not be laughing-stocks to other men's humours; I beg you in friendship, and I will one way or another make you amends.
[Aloud] I will knock your urinals about your knave's coxcomb
[for missing your meetings and appointments].
CAIUS. Devil! — Jack Rugby — my host of the Garter — have I not waited for him to kill him? Have I not, at the place I did appoint?
EVANS. As I am a Christian's soul, now, look you, this is the appointed place: I'll be judged by my host of the Garter.
HOST. Peace, I say, Gallia and Gaul, French and Welsh, soul-curer and body-curer!
CAIUS. Yes, that is very good; excellent.

HOST. Peace, I say! Hear mine host of the Garter. Am I politic? Am I subtle? Am I a Machiavel? Shall I lose my doctor? No; he gives me the potions and the motions. Shall I lose my parson, my priest, my Sir Hugh? No; he gives me the proverbs and the no-verbs. [Give me your hand, terrestrial; so.] Give me your hand, celestial; so. Boys of art, I have deceived you both; I have directed you to wrong places: your hearts are mighty, your skins are whole, and let burnt sack be the outcome. Come, take their swords to pawn. Follow me, lads of peace; follow, follow, follow.
SHALLOW. Trust me, a mad host. Follow, gentlemen, follow.
SLENDER. [Aside] O sweet Anne Page!
[Exeunt SHALLOW, SLENDER, PAGE, and HOST.]
CAIUS. Ha, do I perceive that? Have you make a fool of us, ha, ha?

EVANS. This is well; he has made us his laughing-stock. — I beg you that we may be friends; and let us knock our brains together to be revenged on this same scab, scurvy, cheating companion, the host of the Garter.
CAIUS. By God, with all my heart. He promise to bring me where Anne Page is; by God, he deceive me too.
EVANS. Well, I will smite his head. Please, follow. [Exeunt.]
NOTES: III, 1

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — _The street, in Windsor._
paragraphs: [Enter MISTRESS PAGE and ROBIN.]
MISTRESS PAGE. No, keep going, little gallant; you used to be a follower, but now you are a leader. Would you rather lead my eyes, or eye your master's heels?
ROBIN. I had rather, indeed, go before you like a man than follow him like a dwarf.
MISTRESS PAGE. O, you are a flattering boy: now I see you'll be a courtier.
[Enter FORD.]
FORD. Well met, Mistress Page. Where are you going?
MISTRESS PAGE. Truly, sir, to see your wife. Is she at home?
FORD. Yes; and as idle as she may hang together, for want of company. I think, if your husbands were dead, you two would marry.
MISTRESS PAGE. Be sure of that — two other husbands.
FORD. Where did you get this pretty weather-cock?
MISTRESS PAGE. I cannot tell what the devil his name is that my husband got him from. — What is your knight's name again, sirrah?
ROBIN. Sir John Falstaff.
FORD. Sir John Falstaff!
MISTRESS PAGE. He, he; I can never hit on his name. There is such a friendship between my good man and him! — Is your wife at home indeed?
FORD. Indeed she is.
MISTRESS PAGE. By your leave, sir: I am sick till I see her.
[Exeunt MISTRESS PAGE and ROBIN.]

FORD. Has Page any brains? Has he any eyes? Has he any thoughts? Surely they sleep; he has no use of them. Why, this boy will carry a letter twenty miles, as easily as a cannon will shoot point-blank twelve score. He pieces out his wife's inclination; he gives her folly motion and advantage: and now she's going to my wife, and Falstaff's boy with her. A man may hear this shower singing in the wind. And Falstaff's boy with her! Good plots, they are laid; and our revolted wives share damnation together. Well; I will catch him, then torture my wife, pluck the borrowed veil of modesty from the supposedly virtuous Mistress Page, expose Page himself for a complacent and willing Actaeon; and to these violent proceedings all my neighbours shall cry aim. [Clock heard.] The clock gives me my cue, and my certainty bids me search: there I shall find Falstaff: I shall rather be praised for this than mocked; for it is as positive as the earth is firm that Falstaff is there: I will go.
[Enter PAGE, SHALLOW, SLENDER, HOST, SIR HUGH EVANS, CAIUS, and RUGBY.]
SHALLOW, PAGE, etc. Well met, Master Ford.
FORD. Trust me, a good company: I have good cheer at home; and I beg you all to come with me.
SHALLOW. I must excuse myself, Master Ford.
SLENDER. And so must I, sir: we have an appointment to dine with Mistress Anne, and I would not break with her for more money than I'll speak of.
SHALLOW. We have been lingering over a match between Anne Page and my cousin Slender, and today we shall have our answer.
SLENDER. I hope I have your good will, father Page.
PAGE. You have, Master Slender; I stand wholly for you: — but my wife, master doctor, is altogether for you.
CAIUS. Yes, by God; and the maid is love-a me: my nurse-a Quickly tell me so mush.

HOST. What do you say to young Master Fenton? He capers, he dances, he has the eyes of youth, he writes verses, he speaks like a feast day, he smells of April and May: he will carry it off, he will carry it off; it's in his buttons; he will carry it.

PAGE. Not with my consent, I promise you. The gentleman is of no fortune: he kept company with the wild prince and Poins; he is of too high a region; he knows too much. No, he shall not knit a knot in his fortunes with the finger of my substance: if he take her, let him take her plainly; the wealth I have waits on my consent, and my consent doesn't go that way.

FORD. I heartily beg some of you to come home with me to dinner: besides your cheer, you shall have sport; I will show you a monster. Master doctor, you shall go; so shall you, Master Page; and you, Sir Hugh.
SHALLOW. Well, fare you well: we shall have the freer wooing at Master Page's. [Exeunt SHALLOW and SLENDER.]
CAIUS. Go home, John Rugby; I come shortly.
[Exit RUGBY.]
HOST. Farewell, my hearts: I will go to my honest knight Falstaff, and drink canary with him. [Exit.]
FORD. [Aside] I think I shall drink in pipe-wine first with him; I'll make him dance. Will you go, gentles?
ALL. Have with you to see this monster. [Exeunt.]
NOTES: III, 2

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 3 — _A room in FORD’S house._
paragraphs: [Enter MISTRESS FORD and MISTRESS PAGE.]
MISTRESS FORD. What, John! What, Robert!
MISTRESS PAGE. Quickly, quickly! — Is the buck-basket—
MISTRESS FORD. I warrant. What, Robin, I say!
[Enter SERVANTS with a basket.]
MISTRESS PAGE. Come, come, come.
MISTRESS FORD. Here, set it down.
MISTRESS PAGE. Give your men their instructions; we must be brief.

MISTRESS FORD. Indeed, as I told you before, John and Robert, be ready here close by in the brew-house; and when I suddenly call you, come out, and, without any pause or stumbling, take this basket on your shoulders: that done, hurry off with it as fast as possible, and carry it among the bleachers in Datchet-mead, and there empty it in the muddy ditch close by the Thames-side.
MISTRESS PAGE. You will do it?
MISTRESS FORD. I have told them over and over; they need no further direction. Be gone, and come when you are called.
[Exeunt SERVANTS.]
MISTRESS PAGE. Here comes little Robin.
[Enter ROBIN.]
MISTRESS FORD. How now, my little hawk-chick! What news do you bring?
ROBIN. My master, Sir John, has come in at your back-door, Mistress Ford, and requests your company.
MISTRESS PAGE. You little Jack-a-Lent, have you been true to us?
ROBIN. Yes, I'll be sworn. My master does not know of your being here, and has threatened to put me into everlasting freedom if I tell you of it; for he swears he'll dismiss me.
MISTRESS PAGE. You are a good boy: this secrecy of yours shall be a tailor to you, and shall make you a new doublet and hose. I'll go and hide myself.
MISTRESS FORD. Do so. Go tell your master I am alone.
[Exit ROBIN.] Mistress Page, remember your cue.
MISTRESS PAGE. I warrant you; if I don't act it, hiss me.
[Exit.]
MISTRESS FORD. Come then: we'll use this unwholesome humidity, this gross watery pumpkin; we'll teach him to know turtle-doves from jays.
[Enter FALSTAFF.]
FALSTAFF. 'Have I caught you, my heavenly jewel?' Why, now let me die, for I have lived long enough: this is the very end of my ambition: O this blessed hour!
MISTRESS FORD. O sweet Sir John!
FALSTAFF. Mistress Ford, I cannot flatter, I cannot prate, Mistress Ford. Now shall I sin in my wish: I wish your husband were dead: I'll say it before the best lord; I would make you my lady.
MISTRESS FORD. I your lady, Sir John! Alas, I should be a pitiful lady!

FALSTAFF. Let the court of France show me such another. I see how your eye would rival the diamond: you have the right arched beauty of brow that becomes the ship-tire, the tire-valiant, or any headdress of Venetian fashion.
MISTRESS FORD. A plain kerchief, Sir John: my brows become nothing else; nor that very well either.

FALSTAFF. By the Lord, you are a traitor to say so: you would make an absolute courtier; and the firm placement of your foot would give an excellent motion to your gait in a semi-circled farthingale. I see what you would be, if Fortune your foe were not, Nature your friend. Come, you cannot hide it.
MISTRESS FORD. Believe me, there's no such thing in me.

FALSTAFF. What made me love you? Let that persuade you there's something extraordinary in you. Come, I cannot dissemble, and say you are this and that, like a many of these lisping hawthorn-buds, that come like women in men's apparel, and smell like Bucklersbury in summertime; I cannot: but I love you; none but you; and you deserve it.
MISTRESS FORD. Do not betray me, sir. I fear you love Mistress Page.
FALSTAFF. You might as well say I love to walk by Counter-gate, which is as hateful to me as the reek of a lime-kiln.
MISTRESS FORD. Well, heaven knows how I love you; and you shall find it out one day.
FALSTAFF. Keep that mind; I'll deserve it.
MISTRESS FORD. No, I must tell you, you do; otherwise I could not be of that mind.
ROBIN. [Within] Mistress Ford, Mistress Ford! Here's Mistress Page at the door, sweating, and panting, and looking wild, and she must speak with you at once.
FALSTAFF. She shall not see me: I'll conceal myself behind the arras.
MISTRESS FORD. Please, do so: she's a very gossipy woman. [FALSTAFF hides himself.]
[Re-enter MISTRESS PAGE and ROBIN.]
What's the matter? How now!
MISTRESS PAGE. O Mistress Ford, what have you done? You are shamed, you are overthrown, you are undone forever!
MISTRESS FORD. What's the matter, good Mistress Page?
MISTRESS PAGE. O alas, Mistress Ford! Having an honest man for your husband, to give him such cause of suspicion!
MISTRESS FORD. What cause of suspicion?
MISTRESS PAGE. What cause of suspicion! Shame on you! How I have been mistaken in you!
MISTRESS FORD. Why, alas, what's the matter?

MISTRESS PAGE. Your husband is coming here, woman, with all the officers in Windsor, to search for a gentleman that he says is here in the house now, with your consent, to take an unfair advantage of his absence: you are ruined.
MISTRESS FORD. It is not so, I hope.

MISTRESS PAGE. Pray heaven it not be so, that you have such a man here! But it's most certain your husband is coming, with half Windsor at his heels, to search for such a man. I came ahead to tell you. If you know yourself clear, why, I am glad of it; but if you have a friend here, convey, convey him out. Don't be paralysed; call all your senses to you; defend your reputation, or bid farewell to your good life forever.
MISTRESS FORD. What shall I do? There is a gentleman, my dear friend; and I do not fear my own shame so much as his peril: I would rather, than a thousand pounds, that he were out of the house.

MISTRESS PAGE. For shame! Never stand on 'you had rather' and 'you had rather:' your husband is at hand; think of some way to get him out: in the house you cannot hide him. O, how you have deceived me! Look, here is a basket: if he is of any reasonable stature, he may creep in here; and throw foul linen upon him, as if it were going to be washed: or — it is bleaching season — send him with your two men to Datchet-mead.
MISTRESS FORD. He's too big to fit in there. What shall I do?
FALSTAFF. [Coming forward] Let me see it, let me see it, O, let me see it! — I'll get in, I'll get in. — Follow your friend's advice. — I'll get in.
MISTRESS PAGE. What, Sir John Falstaff! Are these your letters, knight?
FALSTAFF. I love you. — Help me away. — Let me creep in here. — I'll never—
[Gets into the basket; they cover him with foul linen.]
MISTRESS PAGE. Help to cover your master, boy. — Call your men, Mistress Ford. — You dissembling knight!
MISTRESS FORD. What, John! Robert! John! [Exit ROBIN.]
[Re-enter SERVANTS.]
Go quickly and take up these clothes here. — Where's the cowl-staff? Look how you dawdle! — Carry them to the laundress in Datchet-mead; quickly, come.
[Enter FORD, PAGE, CAIUS, and SIR HUGH EVANS.]
FORD. Please, come close: if I suspect without cause, why then make sport of me; then let me be your jest; I deserve it. — How now! Where are you carrying this?
SERVANT. To the laundress, indeed.
MISTRESS FORD. Why, what business is it of yours where they take it? You'd best meddle with buck-washing.
FORD. Buck! — I wish I could wash myself of the buck! — Buck, buck, buck! Yes, buck; I warrant you, buck; and in season too, it shall appear.
[Exeunt SERVANTS with the basket.]

Gentlemen, I have dreamed tonight; I'll tell you my dream. Here, here, here are my keys: go up to my chambers; search, seek, find out: I warrant we shall unkennel the fox. Let me block this way first. [Locking the door.] So, now uncouple the hounds.
PAGE. Good Master Ford, be content: you wrong yourself too much.
FORD. True, Master Page. Up, gentlemen; you shall see sport shortly: follow me, gentlemen. [Exit.]
EVANS. This is very fantastical humours and jealousies.
CAIUS. By God, it is not the fashion of France; one is not jealous in France.
PAGE. No, follow him, gentlemen; see the result of his search. [Exeunt PAGE, CAIUS, and EVANS.]
MISTRESS PAGE. Is there not a double excellence in this?
MISTRESS FORD. I do not know which pleases me more, that my husband is deceived, or Sir John.
MISTRESS PAGE. What a state he was in when your husband asked who was in the basket!
MISTRESS FORD. I am half afraid he will need washing; so throwing him into the water will do him a favour.
MISTRESS PAGE. Hang him, dishonest rascal! I wish all of the same strain were in the same distress.
MISTRESS FORD. I think my husband has some special suspicion of Falstaff's being here; for I never saw him so gross in his jealousy until now.
MISTRESS PAGE. I will devise a plot to test that; and we shall yet have more tricks with Falstaff: his dissolute disease will hardly obey this single medicine.
MISTRESS FORD. Shall we send that foolish carrion, Mistress Quickly, to him, and excuse his being thrown in the water; and give him another hope, to lead him into another punishment?
MISTRESS PAGE. We will do it: let him be sent for tomorrow, eight o'clock, to have amends.
[Re-enter FORD, PAGE, CAIUS, and SIR HUGH EVANS.]
FORD. I cannot find him: perhaps the knave bragged of what he could not achieve.
MISTRESS PAGE. [Aside to MISTRESS FORD] Did you hear that?
MISTRESS FORD. You treat me well, Master Ford, do you?
FORD. Yes, I do.
MISTRESS FORD. Heaven make you better than your thoughts!
FORD. Amen!
MISTRESS PAGE. You do yourself great wrong, Master Ford.
FORD. Yes, yes; I must bear it.
EVANS. If there be any body in the house, and in the chambers, and in the coffers, and in the presses, heaven forgive my sins at the day of judgement!
CAIUS. By God, nor I either: there are no bodies.
PAGE. Fie, fie, Master Ford! Are you not ashamed? What spirit, what devil suggests this imagination? I would not have your kind of derangement for all the wealth of Windsor Castle.
FORD. It is my fault, Master Page: I suffer for it.
EVANS. You suffer for a bad conscience: your wife is as honest a woman as I would desire among five thousand, and five hundred too.
CAIUS. By God, I see she is an honest woman.

FORD. Well, I promised you a dinner. — Come, come, let's walk in the Park: I beg you, pardon me; I will hereafter let you know why I have done this. — Come, wife; come, Mistress Page. — I beg you, pardon me; please, heartily pardon me.

PAGE. Let's go in, gentlemen; but, trust me, we shall mock him. I invite you tomorrow morning to my house for breakfast: after which, we'll go bird-hunting together; I have a fine hawk for the bush. Shall it be so?
FORD. Anything.
EVANS. If there is one, I shall make two in the company.
CAIUS. If there be one or two, I shall make-a the third.
FORD. Please, go on, Master Page.
EVANS. I pray you now, remember tomorrow about the lousy knave, my host.
CAIUS. That is good; by God, with all my heart!
EVANS. A lousy knave, to make his gibes and his mockeries! [Exeunt.]
NOTES: III, 3
